ACenDon: ReproducDve Health Services Rule (RIN 2900-AS31) 
 
This correspondence is submiCed via regulaDons.gov in response to the proposed 
“ReproducDve Health Services” rule (RIN 2900-AS31) and request for comments published in 90 
FR 36415 on August 4, 2025. This comment is submiCed in my individual capacity and 
organizaDonal aﬃliaDon is included for idenDﬁcaDon purposes only. 
 
The Department proposes to return to its longstanding policy regarding aborDon counseling and 
aborDon procedures that existed prior to an interim ﬁnal rule (IFR) that went into eﬀect in 
September 2022. That rule was issued in response to the Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health 
Organiza8on decision, which overturned Roe v. Wade and rightly returned aborDon policy “to 
the people and their elected representaDves.”1  
 
The IFR removed the VA’s longstanding exclusion on aborDon counseling, and established 
excepDons to the exclusion on aborDons in the medical beneﬁts package for veterans who 
receive care set forth in that package. The IFR also removed the exclusion on aborDon 
counseling and expanded the excepDons to the exclusion on aborDons for Civilian Health and 
Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Aﬀaifs (CHAMPVA) beneﬁciaries. 
 
AborDon is not healthcare, and the VA isn’t authorized to provide it. This comment writes in 
support of the proposed rule returning to longstanding policy that aborDon is not a “needed” 
medical service under Dtle 38 sec 1710.  
 
The 2022 IFR Was Not Jus2ﬁed 
 
The enDre IFR was predicated on assumpDons about how veterans and their beneﬁciaries would 
be aﬀected by post-Dobbs state aborDon restricDons – namely, that there would be a spike in 
demand for VA-covered aborDons. The Department failed to provide evidence for its wild 
predicDon, and as the proposed rule notes, the spike never materialized. In fact, the 
Department never idenDﬁed a single instance since the Dobbs decision of a veteran or covered 
beneﬁciary being denied a medically necessary aborDon. Relying on baseless speculaDon, the 
Department created out of thin air an aborDon on-demand enDtlement for veterans, completely 
ignoring state laws in the process.  
 
Abor2on Hurts – Not Helps – Women

Beyond the physical health risks associated with aborDon,2 it is not uncommon for women to 
experience sustained feelings of regret and loss. Post-aborDve women ocen experience high 
rates of anxiety, depression, substance and alcohol abuse, and thoughts of suicide.3 The IFR 
didn’t consider the physical, emoDonal, or mental harm a veteran or CHAMPVA beneﬁciary may 
suﬀer acer enduring an aborDon. 
 
And since aborDons cost less and require fewer accommodaDons than pregnancy, childbirth, 
and lactaDon, aborDon can be implied (or said outright) to be the “cheap and easy” opDon in 
high-performance, high-stress environments. There’s nothing pro-woman about employees 
feeling that someone in a posiDon of power is pudng a thumb on the scale in favor of aborDon 
over childbirth and parenDng. The IFR failed to consider this disturbing dynamic.  
 
Health Ra2onale Flawed 
 
The Department claimed the IFR was necessary in order to protect the lives and health of 
veterans. But every state aborDon restricDon – including those most protecDve of mothers and 
their unborn children – includes language making clear that doctors may sDll intervene to 
preserve a mother’s life.4 And the Department’s desire to protect health may seem innocuous 
at ﬁrst glance. But when the term “health” is broadly constructed with no qualiﬁcaDon or 
limitaDon, it is not actually a limiDng factor at all.5 In pracDce, the IFR allowed aborDon on-
demand unDl birth, without any gestaDonal limits.  
 
The proposed rule returns to the pre-2022 policy. And under that policy, women can conDnue 
receiving high-quality care just as they did for the many years before the previous 
administraDon set out to resist and undermine the Dobbs decision at every turn.  
 
The 2022 IFR made the uncriDcal assumpDon that aborDons are either the sole or the best 
means of addressing certain pregnancy-related health concerns. This is, of course, not true.  
 
For instance, the IFR cited a variety of pregnancy-related health risks including “hypertension,” 
“hemorrhage,” “newly diagnosed cancer requiring prompt treatment, and intrauterine 
infecDons.” But it is not clear how state restricDons on elecDve aborDons prevent doctors from

For other condiDons unique to pregnancy such as “severe preeclampsia,” “placenta accreta 
spectrum, and peripartum hysterectomy,” the IFR gave no indicaDon of whether aborDons are 
the sole or even the most eﬀecDve means of prevenDng or treaDng these condiDons. Instead, 
the IFR simply speculated that “an aborDon may be the only treatment available to protect the 
health of the pregnant [veteran or] CHAMPVA beneﬁciary.”  
 
Why did the Department say this is so? We don’t know. There was no eﬀort to idenDfy 
situaDons when aborDon is the only treatment available, and there was no eﬀort to determine 
how frequently such situaDons occur. These are criDcally important quesDons and in 2022 the 
Department didn’t even try to answer them. In doing so the Department prevented meaningful 
assessment of, and comment on, the merits of the rule (and the asserDon of good cause).  
 
CitaDons to general studies about mortality rates and pregnancy health risks don’t address the 
speciﬁc claim that veterans and their beneﬁciaries face imminent, unavoidable pregnancy-
related health risks that only an induced aborDon procedure can address. On the contrary, 
doctors rouDnely save pregnant women’s lives – without performing aborDons6 – in the exact 
situaDons the IFR speculated that aborDon could be the only opDon. 
 
What Is – and Isn’t – an Abor2on 
 
As the Department corrects the errors of the previous IFR, it should consider being more explicit 
about deﬁning what an aborDon is, and what it is not. Speciﬁcally, the department should be 
crystal clear that that treatment for ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage are not aborDons, and 
are not – and have never been – aﬀected by the proposed rule.  
 
TreaDng ectopic pregnancy – which can be life-threatening if untreated – is meant to save a 
mother’s life, not directly kill her unborn child. Managing a miscarriage (someDmes called 
“spontaneous aborDon”) is when a woman receives care in the acermath of her child tragically 
dying in utero. AborDon, in contrast, directly and inten8onally kills the unborn child. DisDncDons 
make all the diﬀerence, and the Department should be clear that aborDon, which deliberately 
ends an unborn child’s life, is inherently diﬀerent. 
 
Excep2on Language 
 
The proposal amends § 17.272 to exclude aborDons “except when a physician cerDﬁes that the 
life of the mother would be endangered if the fetus were carried to term.” This language isn’t 
necessary, because lifesaving procedures that separate a pregnant mother and her baby during

If the Department keeps the proposed exclusion language, it should require at least two

cerDﬁcaDon. It should also make clear that vague claims of mental health and stress-related 
concerns do not fall under a health excepDon. In states with vague health excepDons for post-
viability aborDons, the excepDon swallows the rule and a single aborDonist can claim a health 
excepDon for virtually anything. The VA cannot give the aborDon industry such a blatant 
loophole. Many pro-life state laws provide a model to ensure that “health” doesn’t mean 
whatever the local Planned Parenthood wants it to mean in order to claim an excepDon.  
 
Time for the Department to Right a Wrong 
 
It's high Dme the Department return to the pre-2022 policy of not providing and counseling for 
aborDons. The IFR was part of the previous presidenDal administraDon’s larger poliDcal agenda 
to undermine and resist the Dobbs decision – not a measured policy change to provide needed 
healthcare to veterans and their beneﬁciaries.  
 
The previous administraDon started from the premise that post-Dobbs, some states would enact 
protecDve policies for women and unborn babies, therefore “aborDon access” would decrease, 
therefore the VA must step in to ﬁll a “need,” which meant nothing less than aborDon on-
demand at any point in pregnancy. The IFR’s enDre raDonale was speculaDve and driven by pure 
ideology, rendering the whole policymaking exercise unsound from the start. The Department 
should right the wrong by ﬁnalizing this proposed rule.
